arguments.literal: Channel resolution enumerates the published RC tags of the selected namespace (including preserved unqualified historical cuts during a transition), selects the greatest positive ordinal, requires that cut and the current selector to be annotated tags peeling to the same commit, and fails closed when the selector lags or points elsewhere. Channel adoption refuses a same-line target whose ordinal is below the Product Definition's current exact basis; a consumer that intentionally keeps an older cut names that immutable RC URI and digest explicitly and uses exact-basis operations such as sync, not the latest-version channel. Presentation and mutation are separate invocations: the read-only adoption plan binds the current Product Definition bytes and basis to the target immutable cut, annotated tag object, peeled commit, tree and installed-manifest digest and emits a deterministic plan digest; mutation requires that exact digest as the operator's acceptance and re-derives it before changing any Product Definition. Selector, target, manifest or definition drift invalidates the acceptance. A fleet uses one aggregate digest over all exact per-definition plans. Planning inside a mutating invocation is not external presentation and cannot authorise itself.
RELEASE §4; P5, P6, P3; plan hashing and command boundaries are PRODUCT_DEFINITION §4

In a shared release source, an immutable cut binds all of: the Project Release Namespace and owning Product authority; the exact qualified Git ref and annotated tag object; the peeled commit and repository-root tree; the normalised repository-relative Project Subtree root at that commit; the Git tree object at that exact Project Subtree root; the declared Product member inventory and release-scoped claim bytes; and the predecessor and successor dispositions required by §9. The Project Subtree root is a locator inside the exact peeled commit, not Product identity. Its canonical spelling is the slash-separated Git path from the repository root, with no leading or trailing slash and no empty, . or .. component; . alone denotes the repository root. Moving a source project changes this locator and its cut identity without reassigning the Project Release Namespace. A tag over a monorepo commit does not make sibling subtrees Product members. Unrelated sibling bytes remain carrier state outside the declared Product subject. Conversely, a member inventory or payload digest without the qualified ref, commit, Project Subtree root and Project Subtree tree is not a complete reacquirable release identity.
RELEASE §2 Project-subtree release identity; P3, P6

Qualification binds: namespace, qualified immutable RC ref, annotated tag object, peeled commit, repository tree, subtree root and tree, and declared Product member set; the exact release-scoped claim bytes; the governing Product and release basis; each claimed property and its observation boundary; evidence subjects, owner verdicts and unresolved gaps; and the complete successor relation to the declared predecessor (§9). Evidence matches the claim: source success does not prove packaged or installed behaviour, packaging equivalence does not prove semantic behaviour, artifact presence does not prove usability unless presence is the exact claim. An RC is accepted only when the required exact-cut review and operator checks are complete and the human authority accepts that exact subject. If review requires any qualifying-byte change, the verdict stays attached to the old RC and a higher RC is published. Acceptance does not move or rewrite the selector or create another final carrier.
RELEASE §3 Exact-cut qualification; P6, P3, P1; EVALUATION §1 is the generic claim law

The release process has three phases: (1) mutable candidate construction; (2) immutable RC publication and monotonic version-line advancement; (3) exact-cut qualification, acceptance and explicit consumer adoption. There is no second final cut after an accepted RC. Publication immediately makes the new highest ordinal discoverable through the selector; acceptance is a verdict over the exact immutable RC, not a second carrier. If any byte capable of affecting the Product or a release-scoped claim changes, the project publishes and reviews a higher immutable RC instead.
RELEASE §3; P0, P3, P6

Project qualification is prospective. Existing unqualified refs keep their names, objects, peels and public links; a historical tag object may gain an archival ref but is never recreated, re-annotated, moved or replaced. Public logical release URIs stay unchanged (a logical STDO release remains stdo://releases/v<version>-rc.<n>/; the qualified Git ref is transport identity and is not inserted into the URI); resolution binds the logical cut to its exact Git ref and fails closed if one project-local coordinate names different tag objects. Across the transition, latest is the greatest positive RC ordinal over the project's preserved historical and qualified cuts; the first qualified publication creates the qualified selector; the historical unqualified selector stays at its object, ceases to be current for the shared source and is not force-moved.
RELEASE §2 Historical ref and public-URI conservation; P3, P4b, P5

The release-publication context distinguishes seven identities: Project Release Namespace (stable key assigned by the Product release authority to one independently released source project); Project Subtree (exact repository-relative project root and Git tree object for one cut); Candidate Source (mutable state constructing a possible successor); RC Branch (mutable project-qualified carrier for the current candidate window); Immutable RC Cut (annotated project-qualified tag plus exact Product release subject; names one published candidate and, once accepted, one released Product; it realises the release cut); Version-Line Selector (mutable project-qualified tag alias naming the highest-ordinal published immutable RC cut for that project and version line); Release Branch (optional mutable convenience carrier aligned to the selector's commit). Equal version text does not collapse these identities. Branches and the selector may move. An immutable RC tag never moves.
RELEASE §2; P3

During candidate construction: bounded fixes are allowed after intake triage; qualification and operator review may continue; release notes may stay draft until RC publication; the RC branch may move; mutable source is explicitly non-operative for released consumers. The intended Product boundary, release-scoped claims, excluded source-project state and qualification basis become explicit before RC publication. A material scope change is repriced, not silently absorbed.
RELEASE §3 Mutable candidate construction; P0, P2, P6

To publish it, the project: 1. confirms the triaged scope and lawful constitutional re-entry; 2. declares the exact Product release subject and release-scoped claim set; 3. reconciles the release note and other release-facing assets to that subject; 4. runs the proportionate pre-RC qualification and operator checks; 5. commits the exact carrier; 6. resolves and records the exact Project Release Namespace, Project Subtree root and Project Subtree tree; 7. creates one annotated immutable <project>/v<version>-rc.<n> tag and an annotated <project>/v<version> selector tag over that same commit in a shared release source; 8. atomically pushes the carrier, RC branch, immutable RC tag, selector and optional release branch where the transport supports it; 9. verifies remotely that the immutable tag, selector and release branch resolve to the highest published RC commit; and 10. records enough ref, subtree, identity and inventory evidence to reacquire the cut without trusting a mutable checkout. Each published RC tag is immutable. Further work increments <n> on the same version line when the intended line remains applicable. It does not require a minor-version increment merely because review found a bounded repair. A published higher RC without matching selector advancement is an invalid, fail-closed release state; it never authorises resolution of the older cut as the version-line latest.
RELEASE §3 Immutable RC publication; P3, P5, P6

<project> is one explicit Project Release Namespace matching [a-z0-9]+(?:[-_][a-z0-9]+)*, with no slash, unique within the release source, stable for the release line and assigned by the Product release authority; a directory name, display name, definition label, package name or matching version cannot infer or reassign it. A shared release source uses for every future publication: RC branch refs/heads/rc/<project>/<version>; immutable RC cut tag refs/tags/<project>/v<version>-rc.<n>; version-line selector refs/tags/<project>/v<version>; release branch refs/heads/release/<project>/<version>; it does not publish a future cut or selector under unqualified v<version>-rc.<n> or v<version>. A single-project source may keep the unqualified profile only while it has exactly one independently released project and its release record declares that profile; adding a second project requires qualified refs before either publishes another cut. Namespaces distinguish refs; they do not merge Products or imply dependency or composition.
RELEASE §2 Project-qualified Git refs; P3, P6

Advancement: (1) identify the new immutable RC tag, ordinal and peeled commit; (2) confirm no higher ordinal exists on the line; (3) confirm the qualified selector is absent or resolves to a lower ordinal on the same project line; (4) atomically create or force-update the annotated <project>/v<version> selector to the new highest RC commit; (5) create or update release/<project>/<version> to the same commit when used; (6) push carrier, RC branch, RC tag, selector and optional release branch atomically where supported; (7) verify remotely that the selector peels to the highest RC commit and the matching immutable annotated RC tag exists. Advancement is refused when the target has no matching immutable annotated RC tag, any higher ordinal exists, the selector would move to a lower RC, or selector and release branch would not align to the same highest commit. Movement is strictly monotonic by ordinal: a later defect is repaired through a higher immutable RC, never by moving an old RC tag or rolling the selector back. The selector equals v<version>-rc.latest; every concrete RC tag stays addressable.
RELEASE §3 Monotonic version-line advancement; P3, P5

The version-line selector answers only: which highest-ordinal published immutable RC cut currently exists on this version line? It never answers: which exact cut governs this consumer? A Product Definition may keep stdo://channels/<version> as its discovery selector, but its operative basis is the exact stdo://releases/v<version>-rc.<n>/ URI and installed-manifest digest. Moving the Git selector updates no consumer. Adoption is a separate explicit Product-Definition transition that resolves, presents, installs, verifies and pins the selected immutable RC. Resolution requires an annotated selector with a distinct peeled commit; absence of a peeled selector ref fails closed and is never read as a lightweight selector.
RELEASE §4; P6, P3, P5; PRODUCT_DEFINITION §4 installed release basis

A successor identifies the exact predecessor immutable RC whose semantic claims it evolves; that origin stays immutable for the candidate. Every predecessor claim capable of affecting the successor receives one semantic disposition: conserved (the successor retains the claim); superseded (an accepted successor relation replaces it); intentionally removed (current Product authority removes it); or not applicable (no successor effect, with a bounded reason). An unresolved disposition blocks qualification of the affected claim. Conservation is semantic: patch absence does not prove loss when a successor-native realisation preserves behaviour, and naming or code similarity does not prove conservation without relevant evidence. Where a maintenance or support line may affect retained claims, the release basis identifies the watched source, observation boundary, inclusion policy and successor candidate; relevant changes receive semantic disposition at material integration and at exact-cut qualification. The consumer owns its record, branch strategy, comparison and proof mechanism.
RELEASE §9 (STDO-UP-015); P4b, P3, P6, P1

frame_indexes.scope: Release one Product version line and its successor: the seven release identities and project-qualified refs, the subtree-bound cut identity, the three phases (mutable candidate, immutable RC publication with monotonic selector advancement, exact-cut qualification and acceptance), selector versus consumer adoption with its plan digest, and successor baseline conservation (STDO-UP-015). Selected for F-03 task B.
